<reason>Both sides were disciplined and answered pressure questions in proper A1/A2 form, and the debate narrowed cleanly to publication and standardization. PRO won because it steadily forced CON's counterproposal to reveal itself as a mandate with penalties and evaluator-issued documents, leaving only "standardized and public" in dispute, and then gave affirmative reasons for those two features (comparability for deployers, insurance against a captured or slow single regulator, multiplying who can act) that CON never squarely neutralized—CON's reply that "sector regulators" can also see the evidence conceded the point that no outsider can check. CON's strongest material—the sandbox/deployment mismatch and the extracted concession that publication adds no remedy for the regulator itself—was real but blunted by PRO's "complement, not substitute" answer and the "publication multiplies who can act" turn. CON's critique of API-based verification of aggregate results landed partially, but PRO had already specified disclosure of elicitation conditions. PRO's two clipped turns are an execution cost, but the clipped material was marginal. CON argued a coherent alternative but spent much of its case saying PRO hadn't justified "this particular mandate" rather than showing the mandate is net harmful once tiered publication and complementary deployment testing are on the table.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 [A2.1] plus the pressure-question follow-through: casting CON's "enforceable access, mandated testing, required reporting" as the motion renamed, then forcing CON in [B4.1]/[B4.2] to concede statutory powers, fines, published criteria, and written hospital assessments—letting PRO's closing reduce the dispute to "who is allowed to read the results," a framing CON only partially answered with the deployment-mismatch point.</best_rebuttal>
